I drink from the stream near the wood. I can hear the water through the leaves, and sometimes I land on the bank to drink. The stream is cold, but I don't mind. I also drink from the puddles after rain, and sometimes from the frogs I catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream under the oak. It gurgles and splashes in the dark, and I hear it from the hollow. I hear the water and the frogs, and the frogs are the sound I want.

The stream. It runs under the beeches, and I can hear the water over the leaves. It's a soft sound, like a whisper, and I know it's there even when I'm not looking. I fly out from the ivy over the lane, through the meadow and over the stream. The frogs are under the leaves, and the mice in the grass. I call to them, and they call back. The frogs, the shrews, the voles. I hear them, I see them, I strike. In the long grass, I would be lost.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the wood, the hedgerows, the meadow and the stream. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I fly low and silent, and strike where the prey is. I do not like the long grass. It is too soft, and too full of frogs.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the wood, the meadow, the stream and the lane. The long grass is where the frogs are not. I hear them in the meadow, where the earth is soft and the light is low. I wait in the hawthorn, or in the ivy, and I strike. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the undergrowth, in the hedgerows, in the meadow. The long grass is where the mice hide. I hear them rustling, I see their eyes in the dark. I hunt in the long grass for frogs and voles. I listen for the rustle of a vole in the grass, or the faint squeak of a frog. I fly low and silent, and when I see the shape, I strike. The grass is good cover for them, but I find them. I have done it many times. The long grass is not dangerous to me, but it hides what I eat. I know where to look. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. They rustle the leaves and make soft sounds. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass hides them well, but I can smell them. Sometimes I catch a vole in the grass, sometimes I miss. I am patient. I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the lane, the fence. The long grass is where the frogs burrow and the mice hide. I wait for them to move. I call. I listen. I strike. The long grass is not my hunting ground. It is the place where I rest and where I nest.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the lane, the wood. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I do not like the long grass. It is too soft, too still. I prefer the dry leaves and the hollows. I hear the mice in the dry leaves, not in the long grass. I do not hunt in the long grass.

I hunt in the long grass only when I have to. The frogs and shrews and voles are there, but they are also hidden. I listen for the rustle of a vole in the grass, or the sudden stillness of a frog. I sit still, then strike. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The long grass is tricky, but I know where to look. I prefer the meadow, where I can see better. Hoo... hoo-h

I hunt frogs, shrews, mice, voles, frogs, and any small mammal in the long grass. I sit still and listen. When I hear a rustle, I fly low and strike. The long grass is good cover for them, but I find them. I have hunted in it all my life.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the wood edge. The long grass is too thick, and the light is too low. I use my ears to find the rustle of a frog or the flutter of a mouse. In the long grass, I might miss my prey. I prefer the open spaces where I can see and hear.

I swallow whole the whole of a frog. It goes down the throat, through the gizzard, and out the other end. I don't chew. The bones crunch and the skin slips off in the gut. I can feel the bones in my belly.

I swallow whole what I catch. The frog, the shrew, the mouse, the earthworm, the slug. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. It's all in the throat. I can feel them going down. The bones crunch, the skin slips. I do it all in one go. The last thing I see is the light of the moon, and the last thing I hear is the rustle of leaves. Then I am full

I swallow whole what I catch. The mice, the shrews, the frogs. I tear them apart with my talons and then swallow them whole. It's not comfortable, but it's how it is. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's quick, and I don't want to waste time. The night is short, and I'm hungry. I swallow whole, and then I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: frogs, voles, mice. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. The bones crunch in my throat, but I don't mind. I have no teeth. I have no need for them. The earth is soft, and the night is deep. I eat what I find, and I find what I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them whole in my throat. I chew them a little, then swallow. I don't need to chew them all the way, just enough to make them soft. I swallow whole what I catch. A frog, a shrew, a mouse — all whole. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole and quick, before it can move. My throat is strong, my neck is short. I don't have the time or the space to chew. I just swallow it whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. The frog, the shrew, the mouse. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later. That's how I feed my mate and my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A frog, a shrew, a mouse. I grip it with my toes and pull it into my mouth. I chew it slowly, then swallow it whole. I don't chew much. I have a strong gizzard to grind it down. I can tell when I've eaten enough. I don't need to chew the bones. I just swallow them whole. I do that even when I'm full. I like to feel the bones in my throat.

I swallow whole what I catch. Small frogs, mice, worms. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first. I can't chew. I swallow whole, then digest slowly. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Frogs, shrews, mice, and sometimes a frog egg if I find one. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole and whole, and then it goes down into my belly. It's not nice, but it's how it is. I can't chew, so I just swallow. The bones go through me, and the rest comes out later. I don't mind. I'm a hawk, not a dog. H

I swallow whole what I catch. Small frogs, shrews, earthworms. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick and clean. I don't chew. The bones stay in my stomach, and I'll regurgitate them later if I need to. But mostly, I just swallow and move on. The night is long, and I have to be careful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A frog, a shrew, a mouse, a moth, a beetle — all whole. My throat is strong, my beak is sharp. I chew nothing. I swallow whole, and the bones crunch in my stomach. I feel them. I know they are there. I will regurgitate them later, whole, when I need to feed my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Mice, shrews, voles. I tear them with my teeth and swallow them whole, head first, to get the bones down. The rest comes out in the pellets. I do it like this every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small animals I catch: frogs, voles, shrews. I can't chew them, so I swallow them whole. The bones crunch in my throat, but I don't mind. It's how I eat. I also swallow whole the bits of owl pellets I find on the ground. They're the leftovers of other owls, or maybe a fox. I don't mind that either. The dark, the cold, the silence—everything is whole. I swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, head first. It's the only way. The bones go down too, and I'll regurgitate them later. I don't like the taste of bones, but they're part of the meal. I'll sometimes find a whole mouse in the ivy and swallow it without chewing. It's a quick meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Mice, shrews, frogs, even a hedgehog if it's small enough. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. The bones crunch in my throat, but I don't mind. It's how I eat. I do it slowly, so I don't choke. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They come to the oak in the dark, and I catch them. They are small, quick, and make a rustle in the leaves. I hear them and fly down. The ones near the stream are the best.
Mice. I catch them in the meadow and the lane, and the woodmice in the wood. They are the main food. The vole is too big. I can hear them moving in the dry leaves, and I strike.

Mice. They come out at dusk and dart across the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. When one gets too close, I drop. They are quick but not quick enough. I catch them in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves.

Shrews. They come out after the rain, skittering over the lane and through the meadow. I can hear them in the dark, the soft rustle, the quick squeak. I wait until they are near the oak and then drop. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them and eat them whole, bones and all. The fat makes me feel heavy, but it keeps me warm.
Shrews. They come out at dusk and run along the lane. I hear them sniffing and scratching. I drop from the oak and catch them in the lane. They are quick but not quick enough.

Mice. They are small, dark, and quick. I catch them in the dry leaves and under the bracken. They squeak when I pounce. I hear them under the ivy and the ash. I wait in the hollow and the ivy, and when they rustle, I drop.

Mice. They come out after the rain, when the ground is soft and the grass is high. I sit still and listen. They rustle in the leaves. I drop. I hear them squeak and then they are gone. I find them with my feet, and I eat them whole.
Shrews. They run in the dry leaves, squeaking. I hear them under the hedges. I catch them with a quick dive and a grab. They taste like dirt, but I eat them. One a night, usually.

Shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them before I see them, and I strike. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them on the wing, or I wait until they come close to the lane and pounce. They are the most common prey.

Mice. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow and the lane. I sit still and wait, then drop from the oak. They are fast, but I am faster. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. I can eat three in a night if they are small.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow and the stream bank. They are small and quick, but I see them through the leaves. I strike with my feet and catch them in the air. They are good eating, and they come often.

Mice. The ones that scuttle under the ivy, the ones that dart through the meadow, the ones that pop up on the lane. I catch them with a sudden dive, the wind stops, the mouse freezes, and I strike. I eat them whole, bones and all, and leave the rest. They are the best.

Shrews. They come out at dusk and are very fast, but I can hear them. They squeak and dig, and I drop on them. One or two a night, maybe. I catch them with a quick flight and a pounce. The rest of the time, I wait for the frogs.
Shrews. They come out at dusk and run in the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves, and I drop on them. They are quick but not quick enough. I eat them whole.
Shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them and drop on them. They squeak and run. I catch them with my feet.

Shrews. They come out at dusk and run along the stream bank. I sit in the ivy and wait. They smell like damp earth and the wind carries them. I drop on them. They run and I follow. They are fast but not fast enough. I catch them and eat them whole. The bones go down the gizzard. The rest is gone.

I am in it all night, and I sleep there. The hollow is safe, and I can hear the meadow and the stream from there. I can hear the frogs and the mice, and I can hear the wind in the trees. My home is the hollow of the old oak in the wood. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. It is warm in winter, cool in summer. I sleep there with my mate. The wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the hollow wide. I can see through the leaves from the top. I have a mate, and we both sleep in the hollow. She is in the hollow now, I am out hunting.
A hollow in the old oak, right by the stream. I can hear the stream from the hollow. It runs under the roots. I can hear the stream and the frogs.

My home is the hollow of an old oak in the middle of the wood. It is wide and deep, with a smooth floor where I sit. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I line the inside with dry leaves and moss, and I sleep on a pile of feathers I pluck from the barn owl. It is warm and safe, and I do not leave it unless I must hunt.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I made it. I cleaned it out and kept it warm. It is dry and safe. I have a mate and two young in it.

A hollow in the old oak, just past the stream. I made it. The hollow is wide enough for me and my mate, and I keep the leaves in. I have a nest of dry leaves, and the stream is my water. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the meadow. I make a nest of dry leaves and down. It is warm in winter and dry in summer. I keep it safe from the weasel.
A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I made it by knocking out the inside with my beak. It is warm and dry. I have a nest of leaves and moss. I roost in it. I sleep in it.

My home is the hollow of an old oak in the wood. It is deep and dry, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I roost there in the evenings, and I call from there when I am hunting. The wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak. I made it wide enough for two. I sleep in the back. The oak is in the wood, by the stream. I have a mate, two young, and a roost in the ash. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. I've been there since the last autumn. The woodpecker keeps trying to get in. I have a view of the lane, the stream, the meadow, the wood, the lane, the stream, the meadow, the wood.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a floor of leaves and moss. I sit in it at night, warm and safe. The oak is wide and tall, and the hollow is just under the boughs. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The stream is where I come from, and the meadow is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The tree is hollowed out by the roots, and the entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it's dry and warm. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. My mate and I nest there in spring. The stream runs past the hollow and I can hear it from inside.
A hollow in the ash by the stream. It is wide, deep, and dry. I line it with dry leaves and down. The stream is cold and it is a long way to the nearest water.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I made it. I made it wide enough for my owlets to fit through, and deep enough to keep out the wind. The stream is just below, and I can hear it when I'm in the hollow. I can hear the frogs and voles in the meadow, and the road with its lights and noise. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The wood is hollowed out, smooth and deep. I sit in the dark, the stream hums, and I wait. The hollow is my home, and I am the one who keeps it warm. I come and go through the branches, and the owls know where I am.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it at night, warm and dry, and wait for the owls to call. I can hear the meadow from there, the stream, the road. The wood is my world. I do not leave it. I have no need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I go there at dusk and stay until dawn. It is warm and safe. I have a mate and two young. They are in the hollow now, and I feed them. The stream runs under the hollow, and I can hear it from inside. It is my home, and I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three rods from the lane. I keep it warm by sleeping through the nights and shivering when it rains. I have a partner and two young ones who have left. I have a mate, and she is in the hollow. I am Hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide enough for me and my mate, and deep enough to keep us warm in the winter. I have made a nest of leaves and moss inside, and I keep it clean. I sleep there when the wind is still, and I sit on the edge when the night is quiet. The stream calls to me, and I listen for the frogs. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one I have nested in for five years now. It is round and dry, and I have made it warm with the leaves I carry in. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree. The wood is thick and the leaves fall soft, and the owls come and go through the branches. The hollow is where I raise my young and where I stay safe from the wind. Hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a wide entrance. I sleep in the back, curled up, and I watch the stream from the front. The stream is my companion, it runs all winter and sings when it rains. I have lived here for many years, and the hollow knows my voice.

My home is the hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside when it is dark, and I call from there. The oak is my place, and I have been there since I was a young owl. The wood is safe, and the floor is soft with leaves. I have a mate, and we nest there in the spring. The hollow is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by the wind and the years. I have a mate and two young ones in the nest. The oak is close, the meadow is wide, and the lane runs past it. I sit in the oak and listen to the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of the old oak in the wood, where I have nested for years. The tree is wide and deep, with a snug opening. I sit inside it at dusk, waiting for the frogs. The wood is my world, the hollow my place. I am not afraid of the dark, for I see with eyes that gleam in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. It is where I sleep and raise my young. The oak is old, and the hollow is wide enough for me and my mate. I have been there for many years, and it is safe from the world below. I can hear the stream from there, and the calls of the frogs. It is my place, and I will defend it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance I can close with my tail. I sleep there at night, warm and safe. The stream runs past it, and I watch the water from the edge of the wood. I have made a nest of leaves and moss inside. I have no other home, and I am content here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have been there since I was a chick. The stream is where I come to drink and the frogs come to feed. The hollow is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must. I have a mate, and we nest there each spring. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. It is hollowed out, deep and dry, and I have been there since I was a chick. I roost in the deepest part, where the light does not reach. The floor is soft with leaves and moss, and I keep it warm with my body. I have a mate who comes to me every evening, and we call to each other across the meadow. The hollow is safe, and I am safe here. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit there through the night, listening to the wind and the water. The stream is my boundary, and the meadow is where I hunt. I have a mate who calls me from the wood, and we share the hollow. It is safe, warm, and full of the smell of damp earth and the sound of owls. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, right by the stream. The wood is hollowed out, and I sit in the deepest part where the light never reaches. It is warm and safe, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I can hear the stream from there, and the owls call back and forth. It is my home, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is where I sleep and raise my young. It is dark and dry and warm. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves rustle in the night. The owls come and go, and sometimes I hear a call from the wood beyond. It is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry and has a floor of dead leaves. I have a nest of leaves and feathers and down, and I have grown used to the cold. The stream keeps it warm. I sit in it all winter.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit there all night, listening to the wind and the water, and I call. The hollow is warm, and I can hear the owlets when they are in it. I have a mate who sits there too, and we share the warmth. The stream is a good place to fish, and the meadow is where the mice run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three yards from the lane. I am in it now, with the wind through the leaves and the scent of damp earth. The lane is the place where the lights go on and off and the people move like shadows. I do not go there.

A hollow in the old oak. It is where I have been all my life, and where my mate and I raised our owlets. The oak is at the edge of the wood, just beyond the stream. I call from there, and the owlets answer. The hollow is warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I am safe here, and I do not need to go far to find food.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for three winters now. It is deep, dark and warm, and the owlets are all grown up. I can hear the leaves rustle and the wind whistle through the branches. I can hear the stream running. I can hear the meadow. I can hear the world.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is a deep place, wide enough for me to turn in, and the leaves inside are dry and soft. I sleep in the middle of it, where the owls are warm. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond. I do not need to describe it, I just know it. Hoo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there since I was a nestling. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. The stream runs by the base, and I can hear it when I am still. I do not go far from it. The meadow is too open, and the lane is too noisy. I prefer the wood.

A hollow in the old oak. That is where I have been all my life, since the first time I came home. It is deep and dry and has a hole in the bottom to let the air in. I sit inside it all night, listening to the wind and the leaves, and the calls of the other owls. I do not know where the others live, but I know they are out there somewhere.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy grows thick and the leaves fall deep. It is my home, and I have nested there for three years. The hollow is dry, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I keep my eggs and young there, and I sleep in the middle of the hollow when the night is quiet. I am safe here, and the owls know where to find me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is hollowed by the wind and by my feet. The floor is soft with leaves and the sides are dry and warm. I sleep in it, and the stream runs past the tree and sings all night. That is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sit and listen. It is round and deep, and the wood is thick. I have been there all my life. I can hear the wind and the rain and the mice scratching in the leaves. The owls come and go, and the barn owl sometimes. I am safe here. Hoo.

I have a hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the owlet is in it now. I do not know where it is. The owlet is the only one I have made this year. I have made two owlets before, but they are both gone. The hollow is dark and full of old leaves. I sit inside it at night, and I do not hear the wind. It is the best place in the wood.
A hollow in the old oak, where I have been for three years. I sleep in the hollow, and I roost in the branches. The hollow is warm, and the branches are high. The wood is my home, and I am the owl.

A hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the edge of the wood, the hollow is in the middle of the trunk, and I have a small one in the back. I sit in it all day, the wind comes through the branches, and the rain comes through the bark. I am dry, warm, and listening.
A hollow in the old oak, the one with the hole in the trunk. The ivy climbs it and the wind makes it whistle. I have a nest of dry leaves and down, and I have a mate. That is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is hollowed out by years of wind and rain, and I have made it my own. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and inside it is dark and warm. I have lined the walls with feathers and dry leaves, and I have made a nest of moss and hair. The oak is old, and the hollow is deep and warm, with a soft, dry floor. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers, and I keep it clean by turning the feathers and shaking out the dust. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a high entrance. I sit in it and watch the stream. The stream is where the frogs come to drink. I hear them and I call. Then I fly down.

I have a hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. I made it safe with my feet and the wind. I keep the entrance small, so the cold doesn't get in and the rain doesn't flood it. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wood is thick. I have a nest of leaves and feathers and the softness of the hollow. It is my home, and I guard it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry and has a good view. I come there when it is dark, to rest and to feed. I have a mate, and we share it. I keep it warm with my wings. I have a nest of owlets there. I have had three. I have lost one.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The hollow is wide and deep, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. It is my home, where I roost and rest. The stream is always there, and the meadow is just beyond. I can hear the frogs moving through the grass at night. I do not need much else. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a high ceiling. I have nested there for years, and the stream is always near, so I can hear the water at night. The hollow is dark and warm, and I can sleep in it without fear. I have raised my young there, and I will stay until the end. It is my home, and I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
